title: Ἑρμοῦ ἅμαξα καὶ Ἄραβες
part: Hermes' Wagon and the Arabs (Chambry 112 · Perry 309)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 112 (= Perry 309). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἑρμῆς ποτε ἅμαξαν ψευσμάτων καὶ πανουργίας καὶ ἀπάτης μεστὴν διὰ πάσης ἤλαυνε γῆς, κατὰ χώραν μικρόν τε διανέμων τοῦ φόρτου.
sentences.tr: Hermēs pote hamaxan pseusmatōn kai panourgias kai apatēs mestēn dia pasēs ēlaune gēs, kata chōran mikron te dianemōn tou phortou.
sentences.l: Hermes once was driving through all the earth a wagon full of lies and knavery and deceit, dealing out a little of the freight country by country.
sentences.i: Hermes was once driving through the whole earth a wagon loaded with lies, knavery and deceit, and dealing out a little of the freight in each country as he went.
sentences.n: μεστήν takes the genitive of what fills it, and three genitives are heaped up here. διὰ πάσης … γῆς has the preposition parted from its noun by the verb, an ordering Greek allows freely and English cannot copy. κατὰ χώραν is distributive, 'country by country'.

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ εἰς τὴν τῶν Ἀράβων χώραν ἦλθε, λέγεται ἐξαίφνης συντριβῆναι τὴν ἅμαξαν.
sentences.tr: Hōs de eis tēn tōn Arabōn chōran ēlthe, legetai exaiphnēs syntribēnai tēn hamaxan.
sentences.l: And when he came into the land of the Arabs, the wagon is said to have suddenly broken to pieces.
sentences.n: λέγεται with the accusative and infinitive is the impersonal 'it is said that…', by which the teller stands back a pace from his own story. συντριβῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of συντρίβω, to crush together, to shatter.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ ὥσπερ πολύτιμον φόρτον τὰ ἐξ αὐτῆς ἁρπάσαντες οὐκ ἀφῆκαν εἰς ἄλλους ἀνθρώπους προελθεῖν.
sentences.tr: Hoi de hōsper polytimon phorton ta ex autēs harpasantes ouk aphēkan eis allous anthrōpous proelthein.
sentences.l: And they, snatching up the things that came out of it as though they were a costly freight, did not let them go on to other men.
sentences.i: And they seized on the things that had spilled out of it as though they were precious cargo, and never let them pass on to any other people.
sentences.n: τὰ ἐξ αὐτῆς is 'the things out of it': the article turns the prepositional phrase into a noun, a very Greek economy. ἀφῆκαν, aorist of ἀφίημι, 'let go', governs the infinitive προελθεῖν — they did not let it go forward.

sentences.t: Ὅτι Ἄραβες ὑπὲρ πᾶν ἔθνος ψευσταὶ καὶ ἀπατεῶνές εἰσιν· ἐν γλώσσῃ γὰρ αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀλήθεια.
sentences.tr: Hoti Arabes hyper pan ethnos pseustai kai apateōnes eisin· en glōssēi gar autōn ouk estin alētheia.
sentences.l: That the Arabs beyond every nation are liars and cheats; for in their tongue there is no truth.
sentences.i: The story shows that the Arabs beyond every nation are liars and cheats; for in their tongue there is no truth.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. ὑπέρ with the accusative is comparative here, 'beyond, more than'. ἀπατεών is the agent-noun of ἀπατάω, a swindler. The close is a piece of ethnic invective, and it is given as Chambry prints it, unsoftened.
